english: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by $f(x)=\dfrac{5}{4}-4\left(x-\dfrac{5}{4}\right)^{3}$. If $f^{-1}$ is the inverse function of $f$, then the sum of all real numbers $x$ satisfying $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$ is ______.
hindi: माना कि $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, $f(x)=\dfrac{5}{4}-4\left(x-\dfrac{5}{4}\right)^{3}$ द्वारा परिभाषित है। यदि $f^{-1}$, $f$ का प्रतिलोम फलन है, तो समीकरण $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$ को सन्तुष्ट करने वाली सभी वास्तविक संख्याओं $x$ का योग ______ है।
solution: $f'(x)=-12\left(x-\dfrac54\right)^{2}\le0$, zero only at one point, so $f$ is strictly decreasing and onto $\mathbb{R}$: $f^{-1}$ exists
$f$ is decreasing, so the common points of $y=f(x)$ and its mirror image in $y=x$ need not lie on $y=x$
solution_full: $f'(x)=-12\left(x-\dfrac54\right)^{2}\le0$, with equality only at $x=\dfrac54$, so $f$ is strictly decreasing, hence one-one. It is a cubic with negative leading coefficient, so $f(x)\to\mp\infty$ as $x\to\pm\infty$ and, being continuous, $f$ is onto $\mathbb{R}$. Thus $f^{-1}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ exists, and its graph is the reflection of the graph of $f$ in $y=x$.
For an increasing function the two graphs can meet only on $y=x$; here $f$ is decreasing, so common points off $y=x$ are possible and must be looked for.
If $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)=y$, then $y=f(x)$ and $f(y)=x$, so $f(f(x))=x$. Conversely, if $f(f(x))=x$, apply $f^{-1}$: $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$. So the required $x$ are exactly the solutions of $f(f(x))=x$.
Let $u=x-\dfrac54$. Then $f(x)-\dfrac54=-4u^{3}$, so in the variable $u$ the map $f$ is $u\mapsto-4u^{3}$. Applying it twice: $u\mapsto-4(-4u^{3})^{3}=256u^{9}$.
So $f(f(x))=x\iff256u^{9}=u\iff u\left(256u^{8}-1\right)=0\iff u=0$ or $u^{8}=\dfrac{1}{256}=\left(\dfrac12\right)^{8}$. The real solutions are $u=0,\ \dfrac12,\ -\dfrac12$.

The sum is $\dfrac54+\dfrac74+\dfrac34=\dfrac{15}{4}=3.75$. Solving only $f(x)=x$ would give the single root $\dfrac54$ and miss the symmetric pair $\left(\dfrac34,\dfrac74\right)$, $\left(\dfrac74,\dfrac34\right)$.
originality_note: New: a strictly decreasing cubic that is conjugate (by a shift) to u -> -4u^3, so f o f is u -> 256u^9 and the graph of f meets its mirror image at a 2-cycle off the line y = x (way 4, hidden structure). Closest known: (1/16)^x = log_{1/16} x, the classic decreasing case with off-diagonal solutions. Different because: a polynomial with a centre of symmetry is used, the 2-cycle is found algebraically from f(f(x)) = x after the shift, and the trap 'solve f(x) = x only' gives 1.25.

Checked that f is a bijection of R (so f^{-1} is defined on all of R), that f(f(x)) = x has exactly three real roots, and verified each against the explicit inverse with sympy. Changed: No change.
key_step: Recognising that for a decreasing function f(x) = f^{-1}(x) is equivalent to f(f(x)) = x, not to f(x) = x, and solving it after the shift u = x - 5/4.
justification: Two ideas linked: existence and symmetry of the inverse, and the decreasing-function trap that produces solutions off y = x; execution is light after the shift. Comparable to 2023-P2-Q3 (L3), where a range/branch subtlety decides the solution set; numerical format, no options.
blueprint_concepts: Inverse of a function: existence, graph symmetry about y = x

concept_use.Inverse of a function: existence, graph: f is strictly decreasing and onto R, so f^{-1} exists and its graph is the mirror image of the graph of f in y = x; for a decreasing f the common points need not lie on y = x.
concept_use.Solving f(x) = f_inv(x): f(x) = f^{-1}(x) is rewritten as f(f(x)) = x, giving 256u^9 = u and the solutions 3/4, 5/4, 7/4.
